exposure: oasis soundscape components in 3 Algerian oases (Branis; Chetma; M'Chouneche) identified from binaural recordings at 738 stations and 6 soundwalk routes (18 sections); dominant sound category per section - anthrophony vs biophony vs geophony
behaviour_measure: mean walking speed (m/s) per route section = distance / stopwatch-timed duration
measurement_method: observation (stopwatch-timed individual soundwalk with binaural recording)
key_finding: Geophonic and biophonic sound dominance showed a moderate significant negative correlation with mean walking speed while human (anthrophonic) sound was identified as the cause of increased mean walking speed (one-way ANOVA + Tukey post hoc); no significant Spearman correlation for anthrophonic sounds

exposure: approaching-vehicle auditory condition in a virtual replica of two real streets: gasoline combustion engine noise vs electric vehicle noise vs no sound; controlled pass-by recordings at speeds <=30 km/h with 3 speed patterns (constant / slow down / stop)
behaviour_measure: percentage of crossings and crossing response time (moment participant indicated the decision to cross)
key_finding: Crossing decisions were driven mainly by vehicle distance and speed pattern with no apparent influence of the auditory condition (electric vs combustion vs silent) when the vehicle approached from a short distance without visual occlusion

sample_n: NR (numbers of behavioural observation samples per condition given in Table 1; not in excerpt)
exposure: loudspeaker-played sound in a commercial pedestrian street: music (Annie's Wonderland; 100.99 bpm) vs fan sound (highest annoyance rating >6/7) vs no played sound; crossed with bakery food odour present vs absent
behaviour_measure: crowd path (ordinate y at path/longitudinal-line intersections = distance from sensory source); crowd walking speed; duration time per 3 m x 3 m grid
measurement_method: observation (covert behavioural observation on a gridded site)
key_finding: Music significantly attracted crowd paths toward the source; reduced crowd speed (slower with greater proximity) and increased duration time; fan sound pushed paths away; increased speed and decreased duration; bakery odour drew paths closer under both sounds and significantly increased duration; sound x odour interaction on speed and duration was not significant

exposure: perceived quality/quantity of urban green space soundscape rated on a 5-point Likert scale as one of 15 UGS component items (landscape characteristics block) during the COVID-19 pandemic
behaviour_measure: frequency of visits; duration of visits; activity intensity
key_finding: Soundscape (together with green space access and maintenance) significantly predicted perceived physical/mental/social health benefits; but use behaviours (visit frequency; duration; activity intensity) were determined mainly by sociodemographic context and only weakly by UGS components; with place attachment mediating effects on visit frequency and duration

exposure: 22 sounds regularly heard in 6 urban recreational forest parks - natural (birds; insects; dogs; ducks; leaves; wind; water); artificial (mowing; construction; engines; bicycles; speech; children; footsteps; diabolo; trains; automobiles; motorbikes) and musical (square dancing; broadcast music; singing; instruments) - each rated for perceived occurrence; loudness and preference
behaviour_measure: length of stay in the park; visit frequency; park familiarity; presence of companions; type of recreational activity
key_finding: The longer attendees remained in the park the more positive their overall soundscape preference; having companions and specific types of recreational use increased the frequent perception of artificial sounds; and greater park familiarity and older age raised tolerance toward sounds others find annoying

sample_n: 306 valid questionnaires (312 distributed) plus 3 observed residential samples
exposure: perceived acoustic environment rated on a 5-point scale as one residential environmental quality factor in a hierarchical linear model; alongside greening quality; environmental cleanliness; spatial scale; sky openness; vegetation type; facilities
behaviour_measure: activity frequency (1-2 to 7+ times/day); activity duration (<0.5 h to 3 h+); number of activity types (walking; sitting idle; basking; chatting; watching children; chess/cards; dog walking; sightseeing); half-hourly outdoor activity trajectories
measurement_method: self-report + observation (two-day half-hourly behavioural trajectory mapping in ArcMap)
key_finding: Acoustic environment was the environmental quality factor with the strongest influence on elderly emotional status in flat-land enclosed residences (0.167) and emotional status in turn significantly differentiated activity frequency; duration and type - but a direct acoustic-environment-to-behaviour association is not reported in the excerpt
effect_stats: acoustic environment 0.167 (flat land enclosed); greening quality 0.395 (flat land in rows) and 0.230 (mountainous); environmental cleanliness 0.269 (slope); environmental factor contribution to emotional status 39.7% / 23.3% / 8.9% / 20.1%

exposure: stated preference for 16 sounds heard in Beigushan urban forest park - natural (wind; birdsong; insects; rustling leaves; water flow); human activity (conversation; children playing; footsteps; exercise sound) and artificial (traffic; entertainment; device music; construction; machine; broadcast) - on a 5-point scale (-2 to +2)
behaviour_measure: exercise form (slow walking; running; brisk walking; fitness equipment use); exercise intensity; exercise duration; exercise frequency; exercise location; non-exercise activity types
key_finding: Exercise behaviour differentiated soundscape preference - people who slowly walk; run and briskly walk showed stronger preference for natural soundscape while fitness-equipment users were more inclusive of human activity sounds - and exercise intensity and frequency significantly affected audio-visual preferences; whereas overall soundscape preference had only a weak direct effect on exercise feelings (natural sound still positive)

exposure: soundscape perception of a national forest park as a second-order construct with three subdimensions - physical (PSP); psychological (SSP) and regional (RSP) soundscape perception - 13 items on a 5-point Likert scale; park contains both natural and humanistic soundscapes
behaviour_measure: tourists' environmentally responsible behaviour (ERB) including high-effort ERB (HERB); self-report scale adapted from Cheng; items in Appendix A and not shown in excerpt
key_finding: Place attachment mediated the effect of all three soundscape perception subdimensions on high-effort environmentally responsible behaviour and enhancement of psychological soundscape perception (SSP) fostered tourists' ERB via a significant indirect effect
effect_stats: three-factor SP solution explained 67.966% of variance; Cronbach's alpha 0.788-0.828; standardized factor loadings 0.536-0.918; structural model chi2 = 654.856; path coefficients NR (Table 6 not in excerpt)

sample_n: NR (31 monitoring points on a 70 x 70 m grid; ~992 min of audio clips per day over 3 days)
exposure: urban forest park soundscape recorded 6:00-22:00 at 31 grid points (Sony PCM-D100; 44.1 kHz); 52 sound sources classified into natural; traffic; management and recreational sounds; analysed as power spectral density (PSD; 1-11 kHz) and soundscape diversity index (SDI)
behaviour_measure: frequency; duration and relative proportion of recreational sounds by hour and monitoring point (human activity inferred acoustically; no direct observation of people)
measurement_method: sensor (acoustic recording plus panoramic image semantic segmentation)
key_finding: Park PSD and SDI were greatly affected by public recreation behaviours (soundscape dominated by natural and recreational sounds) and some recreation behaviours may alter the vocal behaviour of birds; while high canopy density and tree + lake combinations attracted more birdsong and recreational sounds
